title: How to Not Be Wrong About AI
text:
Overview
This tutorial is a short introduction to research methods you can use to figure out whether AI-based programming tools are helping your team or not. Even if you don’t do such studies yourself, we hope that understanding how they work will help you decide which claims about them to trust. All of the material is available under an open license, and contributions through our repository are welcome. All participants are required to respect our Code of Conduct.
Greg Wilson is a programmer, author, and educator based in Toronto. He was the co-founder and first Executive Director of Software Carpentry and received ACM SIGSOFT’s Influential Educator Award in 2020.

title: 1  Is AI Worth It?
text:
1.1 The Running Case
In early 2023 a team at GitHub published a paper claiming that developers using Copilot completed a programming task 55% faster than those who did not (Peng et al. 2023). Within weeks that number was everywhere: all-hands decks, vendor sites, blog posts calling it a “landmark study.” Executives repeated it to justify buying tools for thousands of developers. Almost nobody asked the question that actually mattered: is 55% even a plausible answer to the question I have?
It turns out the study used 95 people doing one artificial task — building an HTTP server in JavaScript from scratch — for ninety minutes, and it was funded by GitHub, the company that sells Copilot. None of that makes the result wrong. It does mean “55% faster” describes a very narrow slice of what your team does all day, and it may not transfer to your question at all.
This workshop is about learning to answer the question your manager is going to ask you in two weeks:
That question is smaller than it looks, because every word in it is doing hidden work. Worth what? To whom? Compared to what alternative? Over what time period? Most of this workshop is about turning those hidden words into things you can actually measure.
To keep the ideas concrete, every chapter will return to the same situation.
Meridian is a mid-sized company that builds software for supply-chain logistics. Three months ago it rolled out an AI coding assistant to all of its ~200 developers. The CTO now wants to know whether the subscription is paying for itself. Four people have been asked to figure it out:
Each chapter will hand this group a different way of attacking the question. Watch for the moments where Maya, Dev, Jonas, and Priya each feel sure of something — and where the methods in this book show one of them is wrong.

title: 1  Is AI Worth It?
text:
Maya, a staff engineer — skeptical, wants evidence she can defend, and deeply suspicious of vendor numbers.
Dev, the engineering manager who chose the tool — wants a clean dashboard metric he can show the CTO, ideally one that goes up and to the right.
Jonas, a junior developer — the tool’s biggest fan, who genuinely feels faster with it, but has the least experience to judge whether that feeling is right.
Priya, a solutions engineer from the vendor — friendly, knowledgeable, and paid to keep Meridian as a customer.

title: 1  Is AI Worth It?
section: 1.2 Two Ways to Answer the Question
text:
1.2 Two Ways to Answer the Question
When you set out to evaluate a tool, you can do it one of two ways, and the question — not your preference — decides which is right.
Quantitative methods measure things: how long a task takes, how many defects ship, how many pull requests merge in a week. They answer “how much” and “is there a difference.” They only work when you can define and count the thing you care about — which, as the next chapter shows, is harder for “productivity” than most people admit.
Qualitative methods describe things: what developers think of the tool, why a team adopted it and another didn’t, where people get stuck. They answer “why” and “what’s actually happening.” They only work when you can get close enough to real people to see their actual experience, not their survey answers.
Neither is more rigorous than the other. A good program mixes both: qualitative work often finds the right question, and quantitative work answers it. The trap is methodological tribalism — “we only do numbers” or “numbers can’t capture developer experience” — which usually means the speaker would rather not find out something that complicates a decision they’ve already made.

title: 1  Is AI Worth It?
section: 1.3 Why You Can’t Trust the Coverage
text:
1.3 Why You Can’t Trust the Coverage
Most of what you’ll read about AI and developer productivity is filtered through several layers, each of which degrades accuracy:

Journalists read abstracts. Abstracts rarely report limitations, and the story “AI makes developers 55% faster” is a lot more shareable than “one study on one toy task found a speed-up.”
Press releases are marketing. They exist to generate coverage, not accuracy, and they’re written by people whose job is to make the funder look good.
Preprints look just like papers. To a non-specialist, an unreviewed arXiv preprint and a peer-reviewed journal article are indistinguishable — and a large fraction of AI-productivity studies are one, not the other.
Conflict of interest is the norm. A large share of these studies are funded by the companies selling the tools, so the default assumption should be that the deck is stacked, not that it isn’t.

The lesson isn’t “don’t believe anything.” It’s “trace the claim to the evidence, and ask what the evidence can actually support.” That’s the skill this workshop teaches.

title: 1  Is AI Worth It?
text:
1.4 Misconceptions

Peer review means a study is correct.

Peer review filters out obvious errors and implausible claims; it does not certify validity. Reviewers rarely re-run analyses or check the raw data.

A larger sample always makes a study better.

Sample size can’t fix a flawed design. Ten thousand people doing an irrelevant task tell you nothing about the question you actually care about.

Qualitative methods are less rigorous than quantitative methods.

They use different standards of rigor, not lower ones.

One well-designed study settles a question.

A single study reports what happened in one sample under one set of conditions. Findings become trustworthy through replication across different samples, contexts, and teams.

title: 1  Is AI Worth It?
text:
1.5 Check Understanding


What is the difference between a claim and evidence?

A claim is an assertion, such as “AI tools make programmers more productive.” Evidence is what a systematic study produces when it tests that claim, and it varies in quality depending on design, sample, context, and bias. A single study produces evidence for or against a specific claim under specific conditions; it does not prove or disprove the claim in general.



The GitHub Copilot study found a 55% speed increase. Dev says this means AI doubles productivity. Name two specific problems with that interpretation.

First, the study used a single artificial task, which doesn’t represent the range of work developers actually do. Second, “55% faster on one task” is not “doubles overall productivity” — productivity includes far more than task completion time, and the effect on the whole working day is unknown. Third, the study was funded by GitHub, which has a financial interest in Copilot looking effective.



Maya wants to use numbers only; Jonas says developer experience can’t be captured numerically. Who’s right?

Neither. The method follows the question. “How much time does this save?” is a quantitative question; “why do people hesitate to accept suggestions?” is a qualitative one. Dismissing either approach before knowing the question is methodological tribalism, not reasoning.

title: 1  Is AI Worth It?
text:
1.6 Exercises

1.6.1 Restate the Question (10 minutes, solo)
Meridian’s CTO asks, “Are we getting our money’s worth from this AI tool?” Write down three specific, answerable research questions that unpack that vague one — each with the metric you’d need, the comparison you’d make, and the time period you’d look at. Example: “Has median time-to-first-review for pull requests changed since we deployed the tool, compared to the three months before?” Keep them to one sentence each.


1.6.2 Qualitative or Quantitative? (10 minutes, pairs)
For each question below, say whether you’d primarily use qualitative or quantitative methods, and in one sentence why:

Do developers who use the assistant produce fewer defects?
Why do some teams on Meridian’s codebase use the tool daily while others ignore it?
How do developers decide when to trust an AI suggestion versus working it out themselves?
Does code review take less time when reviewers use the assistant?



1.6.3 Spot the Gap (15 minutes, pairs)
Pick one AI-productivity claim you’ve actually heard (for example, “AI cuts onboarding time in half” or “AI-generated code has more security bugs”). Find the study behind it — or the closest thing to one — and list, in one line each: who funded it, what the sample actually was, what task was studied, and what the headline claims versus what the methods actually show. Compare your list with your partner’s; the point is to feel how much a headline hides.




Peng, Sida, Eirini Kalliamvakou, Peter Cihon, and Mert Demirer. 2023. The Impact of AI on Developer Productivity: Evidence from GitHub Copilot. Vol. 06590. https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2302.06590.

title: 2  What “More Productive” Means
text:
2.1 Construct Validity: Does the Number Mean What You Think It Means?
Back at Meridian, Dev has a number for the CTO ready to go: pull requests merged per week. It went up 18% after the AI tool shipped, so the tool is working. Case closed.
Maya asks the one question that stops the room: “Working at what?”
Before you can measure whether AI makes programmers more productive, you have to decide what “productive” means — and that turns out to be the hard part. A 2021 Microsoft paper called SPACE argued that developer productivity has at least five dimensions — satisfaction, performance, activity, communication, and efficiency-and-flow — and that optimizing one (say, commit frequency) routinely degrades the others (Forsgren et al. 2021). If you only measure what is easy to count, you optimize for the wrong thing.
Construct validity is the degree to which a measurement actually captures the concept it is supposed to capture. A metric has high construct validity when changes in the metric reliably reflect changes in the thing you care about.
Productivity is unusually hard to operationalize. In manufacturing it means “widgets per hour” — output and time are both measurable. Software output is not homogeneous: a ten-line bugfix can be worth more than a thousand-line feature, or vice versa. Much of the work is invisible (reading code, reviewing, helping a colleague). The effects are delayed (a shortcut today becomes defects in six months). And most of a developer’s day isn’t even writing code: a field study tracking developers for two weeks found coding occupied roughly a quarter of the day, with meetings and coordination consuming the rest (Meyer et al. 2017).
The consequence: construct validity is usually assumed rather than demonstrated, especially in industry studies. Dev’s “PRs per week” is a perfect example — it’s a number, but it isn’t “productivity.”

title: 2  What “More Productive” Means
section: 2.2 Proxy Metrics and How They Go Wrong
text:
2.2 Proxy Metrics and How They Go Wrong
A proxy metric is a measurable quantity you use as a stand-in for something harder to measure. The usual proxies for developer productivity, and the way each one gets gamed:

Lines of code — incentivizes verbosity; punishes refactoring and deletion. In 1982, Apple tracked LOC until Bill Atkinson deleted ~2,000 lines of QuickDraw in one week and management stopped asking (Sadowski and (eds.) 2019).
Commit frequency — incentivizes small, meaningless commits.
Story points completed — incentivizes inflating the estimates.
Pull requests merged — incentivizes trivial PRs and discourages hard work.
Bugs closed — incentivizes closing without fixing.

There’s a name for the general phenomenon. Goodhart's Law says that when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure (Goodhart 1984). The moment people know they’re being scored on commit count, they make more, smaller commits. The number improves; the work does not. The same trap bedevils AI-productivity studies, which is why the next chapter treats it as the first mistake to watch for.






Note



In the early 1980s, Apple measured programmer productivity by lines of code per day. Bill Atkinson, who wrote the QuickDraw graphics library, once submitted a timesheet showing -2000 lines: he’d replaced 2,000 lines with a faster, shorter algorithm. The metric penalized the improvement (Sadowski and (eds.) 2019).

title: 2  What “More Productive” Means
text:
2.3 Watch the “10x Programmer” Collapse
The best way to see that “productivity” is a definition, not a fact, is to do the arithmetic yourself. In 2000 Lutz Prechelt measured a mix of students and professionals, using seven different languages, as they each solved the same small algorithmic problem (Prechelt 2000). The raw data is in data/prechelt.csv — one row per person, with the language (lang), work time in hours (whours), and several quality metrics.
Start with the crudest possible claim: the fastest programmer is N times faster than the slowest. Compute the minimum and maximum work time and take the ratio. You’ll get something like 105x. Is there really a 105x programmer? Almost certainly not — that ratio compares the single fastest person to the single slowest, and the slowest “came back every day for a week.”
Now tighten the definition the way a careful researcher would:

Homogeneous language. The mix of seven languages confounds the comparison (some languages suit the task better). Filter to just the Java rows. The ratio drops to about 17x.
Compare the top 10% to the ordinary, not the worst. “Faster than normal programmers” should mean “faster than the slower half.” Compare the median of the top 10% (the 5th percentile) to the median of the bottom half (the 75th percentile). The ratio drops again — to around 11x, and under some reasonable definitions to 5x.
Factor in quality. “Productivity” isn’t just speed — it’s value per effort. The z1000rel column is a reliability score (100 is perfect, lower means more defects), and z1000mem is memory use. Once you fold in “did it actually work?”, the picture changes again.

The lesson isn’t “there are no fast programmers.” It’s that the answer depends on the question, and a number that moves by a factor of 20 depending on how you ask is not a fact about the world — it’s a fact about your definition.

title: 2  What “More Productive” Means
section: 2.4 The Grown-Up Version: SPACE and DORA
text:
2.4 The Grown-Up Version: SPACE and DORA
If single metrics are hopeless, what do serious teams use?
SPACE (Satisfaction-and-well-being, Performance, Activity, Communication, Efficiency-and-flow) is a framework for remembering that productivity has multiple dimensions and that they trade off (Forsgren et al. 2021). DORA — the DevOps Research and Assessment program — found four metrics that correlate with organizational delivery performance: deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate, and time to restore service (Forsgren et al. 2018). DORA metrics have better construct validity than raw activity counts because they tie to customer outcomes rather than to keystrokes.
Both are still imperfect. A team can score beautifully on DORA while building the wrong product, and neither framework will tell you whether the AI tool — specifically — is helping. What they give you is the right question to ask: which dimension are we trying to move, and how would we know?

title: 2  What “More Productive” Means
text:
2.5 Misconceptions

Writing more code means being more productive.

Wrong in both directions: deleting a thousand lines of tangled code and replacing them with a hundred clear ones improves the codebase, not harms it.

If a metric improves, the thing it measures must be improving.

Goodhart’s Law kicks in the moment people know they’re being measured. Better-looking numbers are often just behavior change around the measurement.

Productivity is an objective property you can measure with the right data.

Every operationalization embeds a choice about what matters — speed, quality, satisfaction, business value. Those are values choices, not measurement problems.

DORA metrics measure individual developer productivity.

They measure team and organizational delivery. Using them to grade an individual conflates levels of analysis and ignores the system factors that dominate individual variation.

Better measurement tools produce better management.

Measurement is not management. Even complete data needs judgment to act on, and improving productivity requires behavior change, not more dashboards (Sadowski and (eds.) 2019).

title: 2  What “More Productive” Means
text:
2.6 Check Understanding


What is construct validity, and why does it matter for a productivity metric?

Construct validity is how well a measurement captures the concept it’s meant to represent. It matters because a low-validity metric will mislead you: you can improve the number without improving the thing you care about. “Commits per day” has low construct validity — developers can raise it while becoming less productive.



Dev says “PRs merged per week went up 18%, so the tool is working.” Give two specific threats to that conclusion.

First, PRs-per-week is a low-validity proxy: developers respond to being measured by splitting work into smaller PRs without delivering more value. Second, it’s a before-and-after comparison with no control group, so any concurrent change (team growth, a new CI, a backlog cleanup) could explain the rise.



In the Prechelt data, why does the “fastest vs slowest” ratio (about 105x) overstate real differences between programmers?

Because it compares the single fastest person to the single slowest, and the slowest person is an outlier who took “every day for a week.” Tightening the definition — restricting to one language, comparing the top 10% to the typical programmer rather than the worst, and folding in quality — collapses the ratio to roughly 5x–17x. The headline number is an artifact of the definition.

title: 2  What “More Productive” Means
text:
2.7 Exercises

2.7.1 The Prechelt Data Lab (25 minutes, solo or pairs)
Load data/prechelt.csv into a spreadsheet or a short script. Compute, and write down each number:

The min and max whours, and their ratio.
The same ratio restricted to lang == "Java".
The 5th and 75th percentiles of whours across all rows, and their ratio.
The same percentiles restricted to Java, and their ratio.

Then answer in one sentence: which of these is the “right” answer to “how much faster is a fast programmer than a normal one” — and why does it depend on your definition?


2.7.2 Operationalize It (15 minutes, pairs)
Pick one of — code quality, developer satisfaction, onboarding effectiveness — and write a specific, measurable definition for it. Then write one paragraph on how your definition could be gamed (i.e., improved without the underlying thing improving). Trade with a partner and try to game their definition.


2.7.3 Goodhart in the Wild (10 minutes, solo)
Think of a metric you’ve seen used to judge developer performance. Describe one concrete way someone could improve the number without improving the work. If you can’t think of one from your own job, use “number of tickets closed per sprint.”

title: 3  How Studies Go Wrong
text:
3.1 Timing Artificial Tasks
Meridian’s team spends an afternoon reading the vendor’s evidence pack. Priya walks them through a dozen charts, each one showing the tool in a flattering light. Maya, Dev, and Jonas each find themselves nodding at a different chart — for a different bad reason.
The traps below are the most common ways AI-productivity studies go wrong. At least one of them is almost certainly operating in your organization right now. Each has a one-line tell — a phrase or number that should make you reach for this chapter.
The famous “55% faster” result came from a single greenfield task: implement an HTTP server in JavaScript, from scratch, in ninety minutes (Peng et al. 2023). Real software development is navigating a codebase someone else wrote, interpreting an ambiguous ticket, coordinating with three colleagues, and sitting in four meetings. Speed on a toy task doesn’t predict speed on any of that.
Tell: the task is greenfield, time-boxed to under a day, and done by developers with no other obligations. Jonas is the character most likely to fall for this — toy tasks are exactly where the tool makes him feel fast.

title: 3  How Studies Go Wrong
text:
3.2 Measuring Only the Easy Half
Code generation gets faster, and that half is easy to measure. The other half is harder: time spent reviewing AI output for correctness, time lost debugging confident-but-wrong suggestions, security holes in plausible-looking code, and technical debt from suggestions that solved the immediate problem while ignoring the design around it (Pearce et al. 2022). A 2025 evaluation of five major LLMs found that none produced web-application code meeting industry security standards (Dora et al. 2025). If AI raises code volume without raising review capacity, cycle time can worsen.
Tell: the study measures time-to-first-code, not time-to-merged, and never mentions review, defects, or rework. Dev’s dashboard — PRs merged — is this trap in spreadsheet form.

title: 3  How Studies Go Wrong
text:
3.3 Before/After With No Control Group
You roll out the tool in January; by June, PRs ship faster. Also between January and June: you hired three developers, rewrote the CI pipeline, and switched cloud providers. Without a group that didn’t get the tool, you can’t separate the AI effect from everything else that changed.
Tell: there is no comparison team, or the “control” is the same team in the past. Dev’s “PRs up 18%” is a before/after with no counterfactual.

title: 3  How Studies Go Wrong
section: 3.4 Asking Developers If They Feel More Productive
text:
3.4 Asking Developers If They Feel More Productive
“87% of developers report feeling more productive with AI” gets cited as proof that the tool works (Liang et al. 2024). Three things make self-report systematically misleading: the novelty effect (new tools feel fast until the shine wears off), the Hawthorne effect (people perform differently when observed), and social desirability bias (people tell the survey what it wants to hear, especially when management picked the tool). Feeling faster isn’t being faster.
Tell: the headline number is “X% report feeling more productive,” not a measured outcome. Jonas is the poster child for this one.

title: 3  How Studies Go Wrong
section: 3.5 Treating Adoption Rate as a Success Metric
text:
3.5 Treating Adoption Rate as a Success Metric
“We’ve hit 90% adoption across engineering” is a procurement outcome, not a productivity outcome. Adoption measures whether the tool is installed and opened — not whether suggestions are useful, whether they’re accepted thoughtlessly, or whether the accepted ones are correct. Adoption is easier to measure than benefit, which is exactly why it gets reported instead.
Tell: the number is “adoption,” “seats,” or “activation,” not any outcome. Priya leads with this chart.

title: 3  How Studies Go Wrong
text:
3.6 Comparing Volunteers to Non-Volunteers
A study that compares developers who chose to use AI against those who didn’t is comparing two different populations, not two conditions. Early adopters are more motivated to experiment, more comfortable with new tools, and more likely to already be high performers. Selection bias means any difference may be a property of the person, not the tool. This is the single most common flaw in industry AI-productivity reports — a two-year longitudinal study found Copilot users were already more active than non-users before the tool was introduced (Stray et al. 2026).
Tell: the groups self-selected; nobody was randomly assigned. If Dev had let developers “opt in” to the rollout, his numbers would carry this flaw.

title: 3  How Studies Go Wrong
section: 3.7 Treating Suggestion Acceptance Rate as a Quality Signal
text:
3.7 Treating Suggestion Acceptance Rate as a Quality Signal
Assistants report what fraction of their suggestions developers accept, and vendors present a rising acceptance rate as a quality improvement. Acceptance measures whether the code looked plausible enough to press Tab — not whether it was correct, secure, or maintainable. Field reports from companies like ZoomInfo lean on acceptance-rate figures for exactly this reason (Bakal et al. 2025). Under time pressure, developers accept more suggestions, including insecure ones (Pearce et al. 2022).
Tell: the metric is “acceptance rate” or “suggestions shown.” A rising acceptance rate is often a signal that people stopped reading.

title: 3  How Studies Go Wrong
text:
3.8 Comparing AI to Nothing
A study that compares AI-assisted developers to a control group using nothing has chosen a baseline that doesn’t exist in practice. Developers without an AI assistant still use Stack Overflow, docs, and their teammates. The relevant question is whether the AI tool beats those alternatives, not whether it beats sitting in silence.
Tell: the control group “used no assistance” rather than “used the tools developers already have.” Any tool looks good against nothing.

title: 3  How Studies Go Wrong
text:
3.9 The Tells at a Glance
Paste this on the wall next to your dashboard:

Greenfield task under a day → artificial task
Time-to-first-code, no review/rework → easy half
No comparison team → no control group
“% report feeling faster” → self-report
“adoption / seats / activation” → procurement, not productivity
Groups self-selected → selection bias
“acceptance rate” → plausibility, not quality
Control used nothing → weak baseline

title: 3  How Studies Go Wrong
text:
3.10 Check Understanding


Your company surveys developers three weeks after rolling out an AI assistant; 78% report feeling more productive. Dev says this proves it works. Name two specific flaws.

First, three weeks falls inside the novelty period, when enthusiasm inflates self-report regardless of real performance. Second, feeling productive is not being productive — self-report is distorted by the Hawthorne effect and social desirability bias, especially when management chose the tool.



A study compares fifty developers who volunteered to use an AI assistant against fifty who didn’t. The AI group closes 25% more tickets. What’s the likely alternative explanation, and what design change fixes it?

Selection bias: volunteers differ from non-volunteers in ways that predict productivity independent of the tool. Random assignment — giving the tool to a random half of developers — makes the groups comparable on average.



A vendor’s acceptance rate rose from 25% to 40% last quarter, which they call a “quality improvement.” What’s wrong with that reading?

Acceptance measures whether a suggestion looked plausible, not whether it was correct, secure, or maintainable. A rise can reflect better suggestions — or more time pressure, simpler tasks, or habituation. Without a separate quality measure, acceptance rate says nothing about whether the code got better.



“We’ll measure lines of code per developer per week, two weeks before and after adoption.” Identify at least two flaws.

Lines of code has low construct validity as a productivity measure, and a two-week window sits entirely inside the novelty period. A better design uses an outcome-linked metric (deployment frequency plus change failure rate, or cycle time) over at least three to six months, with a team that didn’t adopt the tool as a control.

text:
3.11 Exercises

3.11.1 Spot the Trap (20 minutes, pairs)
For each vendor claim below, name the trap from this chapter it’s falling into, and write one sentence on what you’d need to see to actually evaluate it:

“Teams using our assistant merged 23% more pull requests last quarter.”
“92% of developers say they feel more productive with our tool.”
“Our acceptance rate hit 41%, up from 27% a year ago.”
“Adoption across your engineering org is now 88%.”
“In our study, developers with the tool finished a coding task 30% faster than those without it.”



3.11.2 Audit Your Own Dashboard (15 minutes, solo)
List three metrics your organization currently uses (or has recently used) to judge a tool or process change. For each, name the trap from this chapter it falls into — or, if it avoids them all, say in one sentence why.

A company plans to “survey developers about perceived productivity after two weeks, compare to a pre-adoption survey, and report the percentage who feel more productive.” Identify three problems, then in a few sentences describe a better design: what to measure, over what period, and how to build a comparison group.

title: 4  Reading a Study
text:
4.1 The Checklist
Maya is the one on Meridian’s team who actually reads the papers the vendor cites. Her secret is that she doesn’t read them front to back — she reads them out of order, hunting for the weakest link. This chapter is that skill, compressed into a checklist you can run in about ten minutes.
The stakes are higher than they look. A 2023 McKinsey report proposed dozens of metrics for measuring individual developer productivity and was widely cited by managers as justification for tracking people (Elsayed et al. 2023). Kent Beck — one of the Agile Manifesto’s authors — wrote a pointed reply: the report treated productivity as an objective fact, when it’s actually a judgment made by people with interests (Beck 2023). The report wasn’t fraudulent. It was confident, plausible, and wrong in ways non-specialists couldn’t easily detect. That’s the failure mode this chapter teaches you to catch.
Run these five questions over any study, in this order. The answer to each is rarely “yes” or “no” — it’s usually “the paper doesn’t say.”

title: 4  Reading a Study
text:
Conclusion validity — Was the sample large enough to detect an effect of the expected size? Are effect sizes reported next to p-values? Were multiple comparisons corrected for?
Internal validity — Is there a control group or credible counterfactual? Were participants randomly assigned? Could novelty, learning, or boredom explain the result? Are confounders addressed?
Construct validity — Is “productivity” (or whatever the headline claims) explicitly and defensibly operationalized? Does the measurement capture what the claim is about?
External validity — Who were the subjects, and do they resemble the population the conclusion addresses? How close is the task to real work? Is the conclusion proportionate to the evidence?
Reporting — Are limitations discussed honestly? Is there a conflict-of-interest disclosure? Has the study been pre-registered or replicated?

title: 4  Reading a Study
section: 4.2 How to Read a Paper (Out of Order)
text:
4.2 How to Read a Paper (Out of Order)
Skip the introduction — it’s usually the last thing written and the most polished. Read instead: abstract → methods → limitations → results → back to the abstract. The methods tell you what the study could establish; the limitations tell you what the authors admit it couldn’t; the results tell you whether the abstract oversold it.

title: 4  Reading a Study
section: 4.3 The Three Ways Papers Fool You
text:
4.3 The Three Ways Papers Fool You
Three habits inflate the published literature, and you should assume at least one is present in any given paper:

HARKing — Hypothesizing After Results are Known. The researcher finds an interesting pattern, then writes the paper as if that pattern was predicted in advance. Tell: vague hypotheses in the intro that become suspiciously specific in the results, no pre-registration.
p-hacking — trying many analyses until one crosses p < 0.05, then reporting only that one. Tell: many conditions with exactly one “significant,” results that depend on dropping a few observations, no correction for multiple comparisons.
Publication bias — journals publish positive results far more often than null ones, so the literature overstates effect sizes. Tell: a field where you’ve never seen a null result.

Pre-registration — committing hypotheses and the analysis plan before data collection — makes the first two visible, which is why its absence is a yellow flag.

title: 4  Reading a Study
text:
4.4 Who Paid for This?
Industry-funded studies in software engineering routinely produce results favorable to their funders — not through fraud, but through design choices, outcome selection, and framing. The Copilot study (Peng et al. 2023) was conducted by GitHub employees and circulated on arXiv before peer review. Ask three questions of any study: Who benefits if this is true? Who paid for it? Who employs the authors? A missing conflict-of-interest statement is itself a finding.
A subtler form of the same problem is flexible operationalization: choosing how to define “productivity” after seeing the data. Prechelt’s dataset produced ratios of 105x, 17x, 11x, or 5x depending on which definition was used — a number you can tune to tell any story you like (Prechelt 2000). A post-hoc operationalization is functionally p-hacking in a costume.

title: 4  Reading a Study
text:
4.5 A Worked Example: The 55% Study
Run the checklist over the Copilot study Meridian keeps citing (Peng et al. 2023):

Conclusion validity — 95 participants on a single task; effect sizes are reported but the design is underpowered to say much about real work.
Internal validity — it was randomized (a strength), but the treatment and control conditions differ in more than the tool (novelty, task setup).
Construct validity — “productivity” is operationalized as time-to-complete on one greenfield task; that’s a thin slice of developer work.
External validity — a ninety-minute HTTP-server task by recruited developers doesn’t generalize to a six-month project on an existing codebase.
Reporting — funded and conducted by GitHub; no independent replication.

Verdict: the study is a real randomized experiment, but its headline number describes a toy task under vendor-friendly conditions — not your team. That one-slide sentence is what “reading a study” is for.

title: 4  Reading a Study
text:
4.6 Misconceptions

Peer review detects p-hacking and HARKing.

Reviewers see the final manuscript, not the analysis history. Without pre-registration or raw data, they can’t tell a clean analysis from one tidied up after the fact.

Pre-registration guarantees a study’s results are valid.

It makes one class of problem visible — undisclosed analysis flexibility — but doesn’t fix flawed designs, bad measurements, or unrepresentative samples.

Industry-funded research is always biased toward favorable results.

“Always” is too strong. The concern is systematic, not universal: on average, funding source predicts outcome in ways independent replication often doesn’t support.

A well-cited paper is probably right.

Papers get cited because they tell a useful story, whether or not it holds up. Many highly-cited results in software engineering have failed to replicate.

title: 4  Reading a Study
text:
4.7 Check Understanding


What’s the difference between p-hacking and HARKing? Can a study do both?

p-hacking is running many analyses and reporting only the one that reaches p < 0.05. HARKing is presenting exploratory findings as if they’d been predicted in advance. A study can do both: explore the data until something is significant, then write the paper as if that was the hypothesis all along.



A paper runs 12 subgroup comparisons and reports one significant at p = 0.04. Should you believe there’s a real effect?

No. With 12 independent tests at α = 0.05, you expect about 0.6 false positives by chance, so one barely-significant result is entirely consistent with noise. The honest response is a multiple-comparisons correction and treating the result as preliminary until replicated.



What is the file-drawer problem, and how does it distort what you read?

Null results tend to go unpublished, so the literature overrepresents positive findings. Reading all the published studies on a topic makes effects look more reliable than they are, because the null studies are sitting in file drawers.



A paper’s RCT shows developers “are more productive” with a tool, and the authors recommend every team adopt it. What’s the problem?

An RCT establishes causation in the studied sample under the studied conditions — usually “faster at one specific task.” Recommending “every team” is an external-validity claim the study can’t support, given its narrow sample, task, and context.

title: 4  Reading a Study
text:
4.8 Exercises

4.8.1 Run the Checklist (25 minutes, pairs)
Take Peng2023 (Peng et al. 2023) or McKinsey2023 (Elsayed et al. 2023), and fill in the five checklist questions above — one sentence per question, each with a specific piece of evidence from the paper. End with a one-slide verdict: “this paper shows X, under conditions Y, and therefore / therefore doesn’t justify Z.”


4.8.2 Find the Spin (15 minutes, solo)
Find any recent paper or industry report on AI and developer productivity. Quote one sentence where the conclusion goes beyond what the methods support (the “spin”), and write one sentence describing what the evidence actually shows.


4.8.3 Funnel-Plot Reading (15 minutes, solo)
Find a meta-analysis of a software-engineering practice (code review, pair programming, TDD) that includes a funnel plot. In two sentences: what does the plot’s shape suggest about publication bias, and how does that change your trust in the reported effect size?

title: 5  Cheap and Fast
text:
5.1 What “Enough” Actually Means
In the early 2000s, Dennis Wixon’s team at Microsoft was evaluating software with the standard usability protocol: run every participant through the full test, compile observations, write a report, and wait for the next release to fix anything. Then they noticed the obvious. The second participant got stuck in the same place as the first. The third got stuck there too. By the time all eight finished, six had hit the same confusing label and abandoned the task the same way — while the team sat in the observation room taking notes for the report they’d write later.
Their response was blunt: fix the label between sessions (Medlock et al. 2002). If the first participant surfaces a serious problem, address it before the second arrives. The remaining participants can then find different problems instead of re-enacting the first. This is the Rapid Iterative Testing and Evaluation (RITE) method, and it captures the argument of this chapter: the point of research is to learn things that improve decisions, and elaborate protocols can get in the way of that goal just as surely as doing nothing.
The question is not “have we done enough research?” but “do we know enough to proceed?” — Erika Hall’s framing: research reduces uncertainty enough to act wisely (Hall 2019). Most decisions about tools and processes are made with almost no evidence at all, so a small, informal study almost always beats a meeting.
The standard for “enough” depends on the decision. Deciding whether to run a larger study: five sessions may do. Deciding whether to mandate a tool across five hundred developers: it won’t. This is the difference between formative and summative evaluation:
Most of what practitioners can do without institutional support is formative — and mislabeling formative evidence as summative is the fastest way to lose credibility.

title: 5  Cheap and Fast
text:
Formative — studying something to improve it. Small samples, rapid iteration, qualitative focus. The question is “what’s wrong?”, not “how often is it wrong?”
Summative — assessing whether something works well enough to deploy. More participants, controlled conditions, quantitative metrics.

title: 5  Cheap and Fast
text:
5.2 Finding Participants Without a Budget
Guerrilla research uses whoever is available and willing — convenience sampling, with all the limitations that implies. That’s fine for formative work, where you’re hunting for problems rather than estimating proportions. Practical recruiting: post in team or community Slack channels, ask colleagues in adjacent teams, or reach out to a handful of actual users. Avoid people you manage or who manage you (power dynamics contaminate the data), colleagues who know your hypothesis (they’ll confirm it), and outliers unless they’re your target.
Aim for people who fit your target profile, not whoever responds first. Recruiting the wrong participants produces findings that are confidently wrong rather than tentatively right. Five participants is typically enough to surface most problems in a focused workflow (Nielsen and Landauer 1993) — but that guideline applies specifically to formative usability testing, not to claims about what “most developers” do.

title: 5  Cheap and Fast
text:
5.3 Running a Think-Aloud Session
A think-aloud protocol asks participants to verbalize their thoughts as they work: “Please say out loud whatever you’re thinking while you do this.” It surfaces reasoning that’s otherwise invisible — what they expected to happen, why they chose an action, when they realized something had gone wrong.
Equipment required: a participant, a computer, and a way to take notes. A screen recorder is useful but optional; you rarely need a full transcript. What matters is what you note during or immediately after.
Task-based testing gives participants concrete, realistic goals rather than open-ended exploration. Open exploration (“just try the tool”) produces impressions; concrete tasks produce observable behavior. Give three to five tasks, realistic and neutral — not designed to make the tool look good or bad. Then watch for: hesitation, backtracking, stated expectations that turn out wrong, indirect routes, and moments of giving up or working around the tool.
During the session, do not help when they get stuck, react to their frustration, or explain what the tool was “supposed” to do. The point is to observe what happens without you, because you won’t be there when real users hit the same wall.






Note



Participants will look to you for reassurance. They’re not doing it right or wrong — they’re showing you what actually happens. “You’re doing great, keep going” is a reasonable response to almost anything.

title: 5  Cheap and Fast
text:
5.4 The RITE Method
Standard usability testing runs everyone through the same protocol and analyzes afterward — right when you need valid estimates, wasteful when participants keep rediscovering the same problem. RITE fixes the problem between sessions (Medlock et al. 2002): run the first session, identify the most severe problem, fix it (or document it as a firm recommendation), then repeat until sessions stop surfacing new problems.
RITE works because formative evaluation is about finding things to fix, not estimating proportions. A session that reveals a new problem beats one that confirms a problem you already know. It is not right when you need to compare two tool versions (you’re changing one between sessions) or a generalizable estimate.

title: 5  Cheap and Fast
text:
5.5 Analyzing What You Found
Take notes during or right after each session, not the next day — memory for specific behavioral moments degrades within hours. Affinity mapping is a simple analysis for small studies: write each observation on a sticky note, cluster related ones, and name each cluster with a claim (“developers hesitate before accepting suggestions they haven’t read”) rather than a label (“trust issues”).
Count how often each problem appeared, and report it honestly: “four of five participants had difficulty with X” is a finding; “80% of developers have difficulty with X” is an overgeneralization from the same data. Then write a two-page report, not a twenty-page one — lead with the decision, list findings by severity, include one representative observation per finding, and end with recommended actions.

title: 5  Cheap and Fast
text:
5.6 Presenting Findings to Skeptics
Some colleagues will dismiss informal research as “not scientific.” They’re not entirely wrong, and conceding that quickly beats arguing the point. Lead with the decision, not the methods: “Before we spend three months on this integration, we watched five developers use a prototype for two afternoons. Here’s what we found.” Acknowledge limitations before someone else does, and present uncertainty as a reason to do more, not a reason to dismiss what you have.
The hardest skeptic is the one using methodological objections as cover for not wanting to find out anything that complicates a decision already made. That’s a political problem, not a research problem — better evidence won’t fix it.

title: 5  Cheap and Fast
text:
5.7 What You Cannot Claim
Five participants can support claims about the existence of specific problems and patterns within the observed sample. It cannot support claims about proportions (“X% of developers have this problem”), causal effects (“the tool causes more bugs”), or comparisons (“tool A is 30% faster than tool B”). The limitation isn’t that small samples produce no information — it’s that they produce adequate evidence for some questions and inadequate evidence for others.

title: 5  Cheap and Fast
text:
5.8 Misconceptions

Five participants is enough for any research question.

Five is enough to surface major problems in a focused formative study — not to make quantitative claims about a population.

Guerrilla research is just asking people what they think.

Systematic observation, structured tasks, consistent note-taking, and disciplined analysis are what separate research from anecdote.

If participants complete the task, there is no problem.

People often finish while confused, backtracking, and making wrong assumptions that happen not to matter for that one task.

You should tell participants what you’re studying so they can help.

Telling them your hypothesis primes them to confirm it. Give them tasks, not hypotheses.

title: 5  Cheap and Fast
text:
5.9 Check Understanding


A team wants to compare two AI assistants with five participants and half a day. Should they use RITE? Why not?

No. RITE is for formative evaluation of a single product — you change the tool between sessions, which makes those sessions incomparable. For a comparison, each participant should use both tools on equivalent tasks in counterbalanced order, and you report what you observe without claiming statistical validity.



Three of five participants got confused at the same step. Someone wants to write “60% of developers will have this problem.” What’s wrong, and how to rewrite it?

A proportion from a sample of five carries a confidence interval so wide (roughly 15%–95%) that “60%” implies precision it can’t support — and “developers” implies generalizability a convenience sample doesn’t have. Honest rewrite: “In three of five sessions, participants had difficulty at this step.”



Why is think-aloud usually more informative than asking people afterward what they found difficult?

Post-task recall is unreliable: people forget confusion they recovered from, summarize impressions instead of specific events, and rationalize behavior. The think-aloud captures real-time reactions — including confusion that was later resolved and wrong assumptions that happened not to fail.

title: 5  Cheap and Fast
text:
5.10 Exercises

5.10.1 Design a Think-Aloud Session (20 minutes, pairs)
Your team is considering switching code-review tools. Write a plan for a 45-minute think-aloud: three tasks you’d give, a recruitment message for five colleagues on another team, and a simple note-taking template for hesitations, errors, and completions. Then name one element of your design that might bias your observations and how you’d address it.


5.10.2 Run a Live Think-Aloud (30 minutes, pairs)
Pair up. One of you is the researcher, the other the participant. The participant takes a small real task — summarize a pull request, or write a short function — using the AI assistant you actually have access to, thinking aloud throughout. The researcher uses the note-taking template from the previous exercise and does not help. Swap roles. Then compare notes: what did each of you feel was hard, versus what did the other person observe as hard?


5.10.3 Respond to a Skeptic (15 minutes, solo)
A colleague says: “This is too informal to be useful. To study whether this tool helps, we need a controlled experiment with random assignment and statistical analysis — anything less is anecdote.” Write two paragraphs: one acknowledging the legitimate concern, one explaining when informal evidence is more useful than waiting for the resources to run a formal study.




Hall, Erika. 2019. Just Enough Research. A Book Apart. ISBN 9781952616082.


Medlock, Michael C., Dennis Wixon, Mark Terrano, Ramon Ruflair, and Darrell Vaughan. 2002. “Using the RITE Method to Improve Products: A Definition and a Case Study.” Proc. Usability Professionals Association Conference.


Nielsen, Jakob, and Thomas K. Landauer. 1993. “A Mathematical Model of the Finding of Usability Problems.” Proc. INTERACT’93 and CHI’93 213: 1993. https://doi.org/10.1145/169059.169166.

title: 6  Designing a Study
text:
6.1 Qualitative Methods: Interviews and Surveys
Jonas has been pushed past his comfort zone. “OK,” he says to Maya, “we can’t just watch five people and we can’t just read the vendor’s studies. So how do we actually find out whether this tool helps?” This chapter is the answer: the three families of method you can reach for, and the small amount of statistics you need to use them without fooling yourself.
The right method follows the question, not your preference. “Is there a difference?” calls for an experiment. “Why does this happen?” calls for interviews. “What patterns exist in our codebase?” calls for an observational study. No single method answers all questions, which is why serious programs mix them.
Use qualitative methods when you don’t yet know what to measure, when the phenomenon is about meaning and context, or when you need to understand why rather than that.
Interviews come in three kinds. Structured uses a fixed script; unstructured follows the participant’s lead; semi-structured — the workhorse — has a guide but allows follow-up. Ask open questions (“tell me about a time the suggestion was wrong in a way that surprised you”), probe what they say (“you mentioned you don’t trust it for security — can you say more?”), and avoid leading questions (“don’t you find it faster?”) and hypotheticals (“would you use it if…”) — people are poor predictors of their own behavior.
Surveys trade depth for breadth. Likert scales (“strongly agree” to “strongly disagree”) are common but have known problems; use at least five points. Watch the sampling strategy: a convenience sample (whoever responds) is usually biased toward engaged users, and a low response rate can produce non-response bias larger than sampling error. Pilot with three to five people before distributing.
Thematic analysis is how you turn interview data into findings. Open coding tags segments with labels close to what people said — use gerund coding (actions, not nouns): “switching off suggestions after a bad experience,” not “negative attitude.” Axial coding groups codes into themes that make a claim (“developers trust AI for syntax but not for logic”), and you keep collecting until you reach saturation — new data stops producing new codes.

title: 6  Designing a Study
text:
6.2 Controlled Experiments
A controlled experiment manipulates a variable and measures the effect while holding everything else constant. The treatment group gets the intervention; the control group doesn’t. Randomization — assigning people to conditions by chance — is what makes causal claims defensible, because it spreads unknown confounders evenly across the groups.
Two ideas carry the statistics. The null hypothesis (H₀) is “no effect.” A p-value is the probability of seeing data at least this extreme if H₀ were true. Crucially, it is not the probability the result is wrong, and p < 0.05 is a 1920s convention, not a law of nature. You never prove an effect exists; you either reject H₀ or fail to reject it — and failing to reject doesn’t mean “no effect,” it may just mean your study was underpowered.
Significance says whether an effect is likely real; effect size says how big it is. Cohen's d measures the difference between two means in standard-deviation units — 0.2 small, 0.5 medium, 0.8 large. A huge sample can find a “significant” effect that’s too small to matter, which is why effect size should always travel with the p-value.
Statistical power is the probability of detecting an effect that’s actually there. Most software-engineering experiments are dramatically underpowered (Kampenes et al. 2007) — a typical 20–50 participants can only reliably detect a large effect (d > 0.8). The required sample size for a two-sample t-test is roughly
\[ n = 2 (z_\alpha + z_\beta)^2 \sigma^2 / \delta^2 \]
where δ is the smallest difference you care about, σ is the population standard deviation, z_α = 1.96 (for α = 0.05), and z_β = 0.84 (for 80% power). Calculate this before running the study, not after.
Blocking handles a known nuisance variable (like experience) by grouping people into strata before randomizing, so the senior developers can’t all land in one group by chance.

title: 6  Designing a Study
text:
6.3 Observational and Natural Experiments
An observational study measures the world as it is, without assigning anyone to anything. Mining software repositories (MSR) — extracting data from git history, issue trackers, and CI logs — is the most common form, and it’s full of traps: GitHub projects are not a representative sample, survivorship bias hides the projects that died, and confounders lurk everywhere.
The trade-off is fundamental. Controlled experiments maximize internal validity but are artificial; observational studies maximize realism but can’t rule out confounders. Quasi-experiments sit between: difference-in-differences compares the change in a treated group against the change in a control group (assuming the two would have changed similarly otherwise); interrupted time series looks for a trend change at the moment an intervention landed. A natural experiment exploits real-world variation that approximates random assignment — say, a tool rolled out to some offices first because of licensing, not because they asked for it.
Finally, correlation is not causation. Three rivals explain any correlation between A and B: A causes B, B causes A, or a third thing C causes both. Randomization is what lets you rule out the last two.

title: 6  Designing a Study
text:
6.4 The Statistics You Actually Need
You don’t need a degree to decode a methods section. The essentials:

Descriptive — mean is sensitive to outliers; the median isn’t. Software data (task times, file sizes, defect counts) is usually right-skewed, so medians and interquartile ranges are usually the honest summary.
Type I vs Type II error — a Type I error is a false positive (rejecting H₀ when it’s true); a Type II error is a false negative (missing a real effect). Power = 1 − β.
Multiple comparisons — run 20 tests at α = 0.05 and you expect one false positive by chance; correct with Bonferroni or false discovery rate control.
Confidence intervals — a 95% CI is usually more informative than a p-value because it shows direction and magnitude.

Worked power example. You want to detect a 3-defect-per-release reduction, and the standard deviation across teams is 4 defects. Plug δ = 3, σ = 4 into the formula: n = 2(1.96 + 0.84)² × 16 / 9 ≈ 28 teams per condition — 56 total. If you can only recruit 10 teams per condition, you’ll likely miss a real effect. Detecting a smaller difference (δ = 1) would need about 251 teams per condition.

title: 6  Designing a Study
text:
6.5 The Four Validity Threats
Every threat to a study’s credibility falls into one of four buckets (Campbell and Stanley 1963; Wohlin et al. 2000):

Conclusion validity — was the analysis right and powerful enough? (underpowering, violated test assumptions, uncorrected multiple comparisons.)
Internal validity — can you conclude the treatment caused the outcome? (confounders, selection bias, novelty, learning, and boredom effects.)
Construct validity — does the measurement capture the concept?
External validity — does it generalize beyond this sample and task?

Many software-engineering experiments have strong internal validity but weak external validity — a randomized trial on students doing a 90-minute toy task may be airtight and tell you almost nothing about your team.

title: 6  Designing a Study
text:
6.6 Misconceptions

p < 0.05 means the result is probably true.

It means the data would be unusual if there were no effect. Whether the result reflects reality also depends on prior plausibility and whether the analysis was pre-specified.

A large sample turns correlation into causation.

Sample size increases precision, not causal warrant. A million-point observational study is still observational.

Not finding a significant effect means the treatment doesn’t work.

It means the data is consistent with no effect. An underpowered study misses real effects all the time.

Qualitative research is just asking people what they think.

Rigorous qualitative work involves systematic collection, structured coding, audit trails, and intercoder reliability.

GitHub data represents software development.

Open-source GitHub projects are a small, self-selected slice of the software actually built. Commercial and embedded code is largely invisible to MSR.

title: 6  Designing a Study
text:
6.7 Check Understanding


A study reports p = 0.03. A colleague says “there’s a 3% chance this result is wrong.” What’s actually correct?

If the null were true, you’d see a result this extreme 3% of the time. The p-value is not the probability the result is a false positive — that also depends on the prior probability an effect exists, which the p-value doesn’t capture.



500 developers using AI commit 8% more often (p = 0.001, Cohen’s d = 0.15). What should you conclude?

Statistically significant but practically tiny: d = 0.15 is below the “small” benchmark, and with 500 participants the study can detect effects too small to matter. Whether an 8% commit bump means anything depends on construct validity — commits are a poor productivity proxy.



Why can’t you conclude “no effect” from a non-significant result?

A non-significant result means the data is consistent with H₀, not that H₀ is true. The study may simply have been underpowered. Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence.



What’s the difference between internal and external validity, and why do they trade off?

Internal validity is whether you can conclude the treatment caused the outcome; external validity is whether the finding generalizes. Randomized experiments maximize internal validity at the cost of artificiality, while observational studies are realistic but can’t rule out confounders. You rarely get both at once.

title: 6  Designing a Study
text:
6.8 Exercises

6.8.1 Power Calculation (15 minutes, solo)
Use n = 2(z_α + z_β)²σ²/δ² with α = 0.05 (z = 1.96) and 80% power (z = 0.84). You want to detect a 3-defect-per-release reduction, σ = 5 defects. Compute the minimum teams per condition. Then say, in one sentence, whether your organization could actually run this study — and what that implies.


6.8.2 Method Match (15 minutes, pairs)
For each question, name the method you’d use and one sentence on why:

Why do some teams at Meridian ignore the AI tool while others use it daily?
Did the tool change time-to-merge across the whole org?
Does the tool’s generated code carry more security bugs than human code?
What actually slows developers down most in their daily work?



6.8.3 Build Your Own (20 minutes, pairs)
Design an experiment for one claim below. Specify treatment and control, how you’d assign participants, what you’d measure and how, a realistic sample size, and two threats to external validity.

Pair programming reduces defect rates.
AI-assisted code review is faster than code review without it.
Developers who write tests first produce better-designed code.





Campbell, Donald T., and Julian C. Stanley. 1963. Experimental and Quasi-Experimental Designs for Research. Houghton Mifflin.


Kampenes, Vigdis By, Tore Dybå, Jo Erskine Hannay, and Dag I. K. Sjøberg. 2007. “A Systematic Review of Effect Size in Software Engineering Experiments.” Information and Software Technology.


Wohlin, Claes, Per Runeson, Martin Höst, Magnus C. Ohlsson, Björn Regnell, and Anders Wesslén. 2000. Experimentation in Software Engineering: An Introduction. Kluwer Academic Publishers. ISBN 9783662693056.

title: 7  Running a Study
text:
7.1 Ethics First
Meridian’s team has learned enough to be dangerous. They know the vendor’s studies have holes, they know how to watch five people, and they know how to design a real experiment. The last thing standing between them and an answer is everything that isn’t the research: ethics, politics, and the discipline of turning “is the tool worth it?” into something with a number on the end.
A 2014 survey of practitioners found they most wanted questions like “how do I improve team productivity?” answered with their own data from their own systems — not controlled experiments or interviews with strangers (Begel and Nagappan 2014). That’s the frame for this chapter: you already have most of what you need; the skill is using it well.
Research on people needs ethical care even when it’s “internal.” “It’s just internal data” is not a free pass — the fact that you already have access doesn’t make using it harmless. Informed consent means people know what’s collected and how it’s used and can withdraw without consequence — and “it’s in the employment contract” is not consent, because the alternative is leaving the job.
When monitoring developers, even with consent, store data locally or give participants control over what’s shared. Monitoring that erodes the psychological safety that predicts team performance defeats the study before it starts. And get legal and HR involved before you collect individual-level data; retroactive approval is harder than proactive review.

title: 7  Running a Study
text:
7.2 Start with Your UX Team
If your organization has a UX (user research) team, give this job to them. UX researchers already do rigorous qualitative work — interviews, think-aloud sessions, thematic analysis — and rigorous quantitative work — usability metrics and the statistics to interpret them. They are already trained to ask “does this actually help people do their work?”, so an AI assessment program is not a new project for them; it’s their existing job pointed at a new tool.
If you don’t have a UX team, the earlier chapters are the toolkit you would otherwise hand them: the cheap-and-fast lesson for formative think-aloud and RITE studies, and the study-design lesson for the statistics to interpret the results. If you do have a UX team but want to check or follow along with their work, the checklist in the reading-studies lesson is what you use to sanity-check their conclusions. Either way, get someone outside your organization to challenge whether your metric actually measures what you care about.

title: 7  Running a Study
text:
7.3 Scoping the Question with GQM
“Does AI make our developers more productive?” can’t be answered until you know what “productive” means, which developers, on which tasks, over what period. The Goal-Question-Metric approach forces the issue (Basili et al. 1994):

Goal — what object, what property, from whose viewpoint, in what context?
Questions — whose answers would tell you whether the goal was met.
Metrics — the specific, operationalized number for each question.

For Meridian: Goal — understand the AI assistant’s effect on delivery speed, from the engineering manager’s view, in the current sprint process. Question 1 — does time-to-merge change after adoption? Metric 1 — median hours from PR open to merge, per sprint. Question 2 — does defect rate change? Metric 2 — bugs filed within 14 days of a merge.
A scoped question looks like: “Did time-to-first-review decrease for PRs submitted after we deployed the tool, compared to the three months before?” One team, one metric, one comparison, one period. If that scoped question doesn’t answer what stakeholders actually need to know, you’ve learned something important before running the study.

title: 7  Running a Study
section: 7.4 Practical Designs You Can Actually Run
text:
7.4 Practical Designs You Can Actually Run
Most practitioners can’t run a randomized trial — no random assignment, no control group, limited time. The realistic alternatives:

Retrospective analysis — study what already happened with data you already have (commit logs, tickets, review comments).
Interrupted time series — treat a policy or tool change as a natural experiment, looking for a trend change at the change point.
Internal survey — a structured survey of your own team, with clear scope and honest limitations.
A/B testing — if you ship software, random assignment of users to conditions is often already in your infrastructure.

Be honest about which design you actually have, not which you wish you had. And invest no more than a quarter of your budget in the first run — the first study rarely answers the question you thought you were asking, and a negative result often tells you what the real question is.

title: 7  Running a Study
text:
7.5 Sharing Results Without Overselling
Every study has limitations; state them before stakeholders ask. Distinguish “we found no effect” from “our study wasn’t designed to detect an effect.” Put confidence intervals, effect sizes, and sample sizes in the report, not just the appendix. And ask, before you send anything, “what happens if this appears on Reddit?”
When you can’t publish, write a memo with methods, results, limitations, and conclusions — and share it with the team that was studied, not just the leadership that commissioned it.

title: 7  Running a Study
text:
7.6 Matching Methods to Questions
As a quick reference:

“Is there a difference?” → controlled experiment or quasi-experiment.
“How large is the difference?” → effect sizes and confidence intervals.
“Why does this happen?” → interviews and observation.
“What do practitioners think?” → surveys.
“What patterns exist in our codebase?” → mining repositories.
“What causes what?” → natural experiments, DiD, ITS — or randomization.

The hardest step is usually the first: translating a vague worry (“is AI bad for us?”) into a specific, answerable question.

title: 7  Running a Study
section: 7.7 What the Evidence Actually Says (and What’s Oversold)
text:
7.7 What the Evidence Actually Says (and What’s Oversold)
Stepping back, the honest summary of AI-productivity research is short: AI tools can speed up specific, well-defined tasks for individual developers; effects on end-to-end delivery are far less studied and less consistent; and nearly all studies are short-term, on narrow or artificial tasks, with volunteers or students. The “55% faster” headline is a task-level result being sold as a workday-level fact.
So when an executive cites a statistic, ask three questions: who funded it, what task was studied, and was there a control group? And when it’s your turn to buy a tool, ask for evidence from a context like yours — not students on toy tasks — with effect sizes and confidence intervals, on outcomes you actually care about.

title: 7  Running a Study
text:
7.8 Signs of Maturity
A team that has stopped asking “does the tool work?” and started asking harder questions is on the right track. Watch for these three:

“How am I going to be measured in my annual performance review?”
“What do we keep when token costs go up 20×?”
“How much should I spend on insurance, and for what?”

The first keeps the tool from becoming a surveillance device; the second keeps you from building your workflow on a cost you don’t control; the third acknowledges liability for generated code. A team asking these is treating AI as a business decision, not a fad.
None of these traps are unique to AI. The same problems — proxy metrics, no control group, selection bias, overclaiming — appear in studies of agile, TDD, and every other practice, and they’re as old as empirical software engineering itself. The fix is to apply what the human sciences already know — which, as above, is usually already sitting in your UX team.

title: 7  Running a Study
text:
7.9 Misconceptions

Internal data has no ethical constraints because the company already owns it.

Collecting data for operations doesn’t authorize using it for research. The intended use matters, and research use needs separate consent and harm review.

A/B testing is a reliable all-purpose tool for internal studies.

It works when random assignment is natural and outcomes are measured automatically. Most questions about developer productivity don’t fit.

Negative results aren’t worth reporting.

A well-run null result prevents acting on a false assumption. Suppressing it recreates the file-drawer problem inside your own organization.

The evidence on AI and developer productivity is settled.

The field is young, dominated by short-term narrow studies, heavily industry-funded, and almost entirely lacking independent replication.

title: 7  Running a Study
text:
7.10 Check Understanding


Why is “it’s in the employment contract” insufficient as a basis for consent?

Consent must be specific, informed, and genuinely voluntary. An employment contract grants broad data-collection rights as a condition of employment, so participants can’t meaningfully withdraw without leaving their job — a power imbalance that undermines voluntariness.



A manager asks you to study “which developers are least productive” using commit data. Name two ethical concerns and one fix for each.

Commit data has low construct validity and can be gamed — use outcome metrics (defect rate, feature delivery time) instead of activity metrics. And ranking “least productive” individuals risks surveillance and discipline — commit in advance that results are for process improvement, not performance management.



A colleague says “hundreds of studies show AI improves productivity — the evidence is overwhelming.” What’s the key concern?

Publication bias: positive results get published, null results don’t. A large count of positive studies may just mean the negative ones are in file drawers. A meta-analysis that corrects for publication bias would give a more reliable picture than a head count.

title: 7  Running a Study
text:
7.11 Exercises

7.11.1 Scope It Down (15 minutes, pairs)
Take one broad question — “does using an AI assistant improve code quality?”, “does test-driven development reduce bugs?”, “does remote work hurt collaboration?” — and write a scoped version answerable in three months with a typical team’s data. Specify the metric, the comparison, and the time period.


7.11.2 Write the Limitations (20 minutes, solo)
You ran an internal A/B test: 30 developers used an AI code-review tool for eight weeks, 30 didn’t, and time-to-merge fell 22% in the treatment group. Write the “Limitations” section — sample size and power, external validity, alternative explanations, and ethics.


7.11.3 The Question Behind the Question (15 minutes, pairs)
A manager says, “We’re spending $X per developer per year on this AI tool. Are we getting our money’s worth?” Restate it as three specific, answerable research questions. For each, name the method and one data source. Then say which question matters most and why.
